en: The Preface: Avalokiteśvara is identical to the self and persons; the self and persons are identical to Avalokiteśvara. This is the dharma of non-duality. The Heart Sūtra is identical to self-nature;
self-nature is identical to the Heart Sūtra. Truly, this is the One Way. The Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya encompasses the cause and penetrates to the fruit. The five aggregates...

Emptiness. All phenomena are empty. Transcending the sages and surpassing the ordinary, emptiness is not different from form. The functions of characteristics and activity follow conditions; form is itself emptiness.
The essence of the single truth is unchanging, neither extinguished nor born. It illuminates the present and shines upon the past, free from dreams and free from conceptualization.
The brilliant sun and bright stars: there is no realm of eye-consciousness, nor is there a realm of mind-consciousness.

Eradicating the characteristics of self and other faculties—this is the Great Divine Mantra, this is the Great Illuminating Mantra. It cuts off the provisional names of "sentient being" and "Buddha," removes all suffering, and reveals the inconceivable power of the Guhyasamāja (Gatyā).
One attains *samyak-saṃbodhi*; the divine efficacy of *svāhā* is unfathomable. To comprehend it in such a manner is to truly contemplate the Heart Sūtra.

To seek outwardly is not to follow the Heart Sutra. It is because sentient beings within the Bodhisattva’s mind have fallen into the ocean of wind and waves of their own *ālaya-vijñāna*, whereby they obscure their innate goodness and forget the fundamental sutra; thus they undergo suffering in vain, entirely without liberation.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva within the weary minds of sentient beings sits upon the peak of the lotus-flower of my flesh-mass, upholding true nature and turning the Great Wheel of Dharma to deliver all from suffering and bring them to the bliss of the second fruit. Since mind, Buddha, and sentient beings possess no separate essence, [they are one].

The words of the Buddha’s sūtras constitute the essence of the mind; how could there be two different meanings? Therefore, in my current commentary on the sūtras, I shall consistently interpret them through understanding and realization.

"Avalokiteśvara" (Guanyin) represents the sovereign mind-king (*cittarāja*); "Śāri" represents the mental factors (*caitta*). The five aggregates (*skandha*) represent the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*) represent the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Thus, one contemplates the mind based upon the teachings.

To exhaustively investigate principle and fully realize one's nature is truly for the purpose of understanding the names of mind and nature. Those who wish to clarify the mind should investigate this text;
those who do not seek to see their nature merely carry a burden of self-conceit. How tragic!
Written on the eleventh day of the tenth month of the Guiwei year of the Kangxi era by the śramaṇa Xufa of Ciyun Jiaoguan,
as the *Lixingjie* (Explanation of the Rational Nature) to the lower fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Xufa, a teacher of the Esoteric and Exoteric Contemplations at Ciyun Temple on the banks of the Qingshui River in Zhejiang.
△ First, the Title of the Sūtra:
*Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
In Sanskrit, *prajñā*; here it is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*). It is the primordial, numinous cognition that illuminates and understands. In the causal stage, it is the mental factor of wisdom;

in the resultant stage, it is the untainted wisdom of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). In Sanskrit, *pāramitā*; here it is translated as "reaching the other shore.
It refers to the ultimate source of both phenomena and principle. In the causal stage, it is the mental factor of meditative concentration; in the resultant stage, it is non-analytical [cessation].
□ Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is the one true *dharmadhātu*. In Sanskrit it is called *ālaya*; here it is translated as the "store-consciousness" (*zàngxīn*).

It is also called *hṛdaya*; here it is translated as the "fleshly heart" (*ròutuánxīn*). The *Awakening of Faith* (*Qǐxìn lùn*) states: "Based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arises the mind of birth-and-death (*utpādanirodha-citta*).
That which is neither born nor extinguished is in union with that which is subject to birth and death; they are neither identical nor different. This is named..."
The ālayavijñāna mind: this mind is inherently possessed by every person. When the mind turns away from prajñā, it becomes deluded regarding the nature of wisdom and dwells on the shore of saṃsāra;

such is called the ignorant person, the deva, the human, or the ordinary worldling (pṛthagjana). When the mind inclines toward prajñā, it awakens to the nature of wisdom and reaches the shore of nirvāṇa;
these are termed the awakened ones, the noble beings of the three vehicles. "Sūtra" means "Dharma" and "eternity."
That which is uniform throughout the ten directions is called the Dharma; that which does not change across the three periods of time is called the Constant.

One who expounds this sutra desires to cause sentient beings to sever the mind of delusive thought, to rely upon these written words to give rise to profound contemplation and insight, and thereby realize the emptiness of true reality.

Awakening to the source of the fundamental mind, one is equal to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the true, eternal Dharma-bliss (thus, in this fundamental scripture, one’s own mind constantly revolves).
△ Next, the Mantra Text.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and distress.

Because he universally contemplates both phenomena and principle and possesses sovereign power in rescuing beings from suffering, he is called "Avalokiteśvara. "Bodhisattva" is translated as "Awakened Being" (*jueshi*) or "Opening Being" (*kaishi*).

This distinguishes the sentient being from non-awakening; it does not refer to mere intellectual enlightenment. Within the person’s mind, the eighth lord—the essence of numinous awareness (*lingzhi*)—dwells within the physical heart-mass.
To enter through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation is called "practice" (*xing*). One gives rise to the wisdom of non-discrimination wherein all phenomena and even that wisdom itself are empty.
It is called "profound" because it distinguishes this from the wisdom of non-discrimination regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, when one’s innate knowledge (*liangzhi*) and innate capacity (*liangneng*) within the mind illuminate and perceive, this is the *prajñā* of contemplation (*guanzhao*).

When these are all empty within the sphere of wisdom (*huixin*), this is the *prajñā* of true reality (*shixiang*). Space is unconditioned (*wuwei*). The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), as well as the phenomena of form and mind belonging to self and others, the sense bases and objects, and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), are all shadows manifested by the mind.
Receiving and experiencing is called sensation (*vedanā*); recollecting and deliberating is called perception (*saṃjñā*); and [volitional] construction is called... [formative action (*saṃskāra*)].
"Forming names" refers to mental factors (*caitta*). "Discriminating names" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

Both belong to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) subject to arising and ceasing, and thus constitute suffering and calamity. "Non-associated formations" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) refer to those who transcend suffering and calamity;

this means that one completely transcends all the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death for oneself and others, just as ice melts into water and no longer undergoes the calamities of the eight cold hells. [The text mentions] the three vehicles and the seven...

They proceed toward [rebirth] and are unable to contemplate emptiness; they undergo the suffering of the aggregates like silkworms weaving cocoons or moths flying into a flame—binding themselves and burning themselves, which is truly pitiable.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "When the flower of awakening is illuminated, one is liberated from suffering and affliction, becoming equal to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara."
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
*Śāriputra* is translated as "Jewel. It is a name for his mother; because her eyes were like jewels, he was born from her, and thus he is called her "son.

This refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). Shi Hu’s translation states: "The World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak, having entered the samādhi of 'Proclaiming the True Dharma through Profound Radiance.
Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: 'If a person wishes...'"
"How should one study when practicing the profound Dharma-gate of Prajñāpāramitā? At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"If you wish to practice and study the profound Prajñāpāramitā, you should contemplate that the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates is entirely empty;
the Buddha is precisely suchness (tathatā) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). The Venerable one then raised a doubt, saying: "Form (rūpa) is a conditioned phenomenon (dharma); how can it be so?"
All are empty. Therefore, the response explains: form is not different from emptiness, because form itself is emptiness.

This means that the illusory, provisional marks of the four great elements are not different from the signless, true emptiness of *prajñā*. One should know that the nature of the non-arising of form is precisely the nature of the non-arising of emptiness;
it is like ice being no different from water: though the characteristics of freezing and melting differ, their nature is one.
In reality, it is one and moist. Furthermore, a question is raised: "Space is a non-existent phenomenon; how can there be form? Therefore, he again provides an explanation:

"Space is not different from form, because space is itself form. This means that the true emptiness of *prajñā* is signless (*animitta*) and not different from the illusory, provisional appearances of the four great elements.
One should know that the nature of non-arising of emptiness is precisely the nature of non-arising of form. As it is said:
Water is not different from ice; water is itself ice. Though their forms differ—melting and freezing—their moist nature is identical.

These four gateways of contemplation are like a great mass of fire: if one is surrounded by it on all four sides, nothing will not be consumed. They are like a cool, refreshing pond: if one approaches it from all four sides, no one will not find joy.
If a practitioner can contemplate the mind through these four propositions in this way, they will immediately transform the eight [consciousnesses].
The Dharma (consisting of the four form-realms and the four formless-realms) constitutes the four wisdoms (via the four gates). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The Bodhisattva contemplates that the bodies of sentient beings each possess a lotus of awakening (the flower of the mind). Within the pure *dharmadhātu*, free from delusion and defilement, there is a Tathāgata upon each of the eight petals (the heart having eight orifices)—that is, the eight consciousnesses transformed into wisdom.
Yet, they give rise to delusion within true emptiness and undergo the suffering of illusory form, like water freezing into ice."—Thus says the Buddha.

Awakening to the illusory nature of form, one attains the bliss of true emptiness; it is like ice melting into water. This applies equally to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which are likewise not different from emptiness.
It is not a case of two separate entities—such as a box and its lid—merely meeting one another; in reality, emptiness is itself sensation.
Perception, volition, and consciousness are like a golden vessel and a lump of clay; they are entirely without two distinct entities that can be found. Thus it is said, "it is also thus.

That "the myriad dharmas are mind-only" and "the mind gives rise to the myriad dharmas"—truly, these words are so! As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Mind (referring to feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness) is also mind-only.
Emptiness (non-mind, referring to form) is also mind; from mind arises all manner of forms and appearances (the nine realms)."
[Regarding] mind and form, one penetrates that they are all merely mind (the emptiness of the ultimate truth).
Śāriputra, this mark of the emptiness of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases.
All phenomena are the five aggregates. In their very essence, they are empty and signless, being solely the primary truth (*paramārtha*).

How could there be arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase or decrease? It is like ice returning to water; one cannot find its melting or freezing, its clarity or darkness, its thickness or thinness.
This is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form; no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
No forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena. No realm of the eye, and so forth, up to and including no realm of mental consciousness.
The essential nature and characteristics of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.

How, then, could the various phenomena of arising and ceasing—such as the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*)—possibly find accommodation within it? Therefore, it is said that "within emptiness there is nothing. This is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) which is immovable and non-extinguishing.

The aggregates are empty, as described above. When form is joined together, it constitutes the eye; the viscous clarity gives rise to seeing. When sound is rolled up, it constitutes the ear; the viscous clarity gives rise to hearing. When fragrance is received, it constitutes the nose;
the viscous clarity gives rise to smelling. When flavor is twisted together, it constitutes the tongue; the viscous clarity gives rise to tasting. When touch is grasped, it constitutes the body;
the viscous clarity gives rise to sensation. When mental objects are gathered, they constitute the mind; the viscous clarity gives rise to cognition. These are the six internal faculties.
Regarding "non-existence": the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "Once one sense-faculty returns to its source, the six sense-faculties become liberation.

It further states, "Because the shapes of the vessels differ, the space within them is named differently; if one sets aside the vessels and contemplates the space, one speaks of space as being one. This refers to that great void space.
What is the same and what is different? How much more so regarding the one and the non-one?
Through the forms of light and darkness, the eye rushes toward visible colors; through the forms of movement and stillness, the ear hears rushing sounds;

through the forms of openness and obstruction, the nose smells rushing fragrances; through the forms of tranquility and change, the tongue tastes rushing flavors; through the forms of separation and union, the body perceives.
Chasing after and contacting [objects] arises from the forms of birth and extinction; the mind cognizes these chasing phenomena—these are the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

Together with the preceding [six internal bases], they are called the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). Regarding "non-existence," the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Cognition is triggered by objects, and appearances arise because of the faculties.

Appearances (the objects) and seeing (the faculties) lack inherent nature; they are like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other. It further says: "Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of form..."
Regarding "emptiness of true reality" (*śūnyatā*) and so forth:

the eye-consciousness discriminates forms; the ear-consciousness discriminates sounds; the nose-consciousness discriminates odors; the tongue-consciousness discriminates tastes; the body-consciousness discriminates tangibles;
and the mental consciousness discriminates phenomena (*dharma*). These are the six consciousnesses therein. With the eye and form as conditions, eye-consciousness arises therein.

These, combined, are called the eighteen *dhātus*. Regarding "non-existence," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky. It further says:
"Since internal and external natures are empty, how could there be an establishment in the middle? Thus, from whom does your consciousness arise, and from what is a realm established?"
Thus one knows that the aggregates, bases, and elements are, in their characteristics, exhausted as illusions and delusions, while in their nature, they are truly empty and quiescent.
They are like a six-colored ice disk with painted birds; at midday, the disk dries and there remains only a vast expanse of water. The wise awaken to this and sigh in wonder;
the foolish merely stare in astonishment and laugh.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to: there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path. There is no wisdom, nor is there attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained.

The dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) consists of twelve factors: first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); third, consciousness (*vijñāna*); fourth, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

fifth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); sixth, contact (*sparśa*); seventh, sensation (*vedanā*); eighth, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); ninth, clinging (*upādāna*); tenth, existence (*bhava*); eleventh, birth (*jāti*); and twelfth, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). These are viewed through two gateways:

first, the gateway of arising (*utpatti-dvāra*), which means "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," and so on, up to "conditioned by birth are aging and death"; second, the gateway of cessation (*nirodha-dvāra*).

The "gate of exhaustion" refers to the cessation of ignorance, which leads to the cessation of volitional formations, and so on, until the cessation of birth, which leads to the cessation of old age and death.
"Exhaustion" (jìn) is synonymous with "cessation" (nirodha). The phrase "and so on" (nǎizhì) indicates an abbreviation that omits the ten intermediate links, citing only the first and last links.

When it is said that these are all "non-existent," one should understand that where there is no ignorance, old age, death, and birth, there is likewise no cessation of ignorance, old age, death, and birth. Since...
There is no ignorance, nor aging, death, or birth; truly, there is no extinction of ignorance, aging, death, or birth.

This is because that which arises through conditions is empty of intrinsic nature, and thus no real entity can be found. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous; its nature is not produced by causes and conditions."
Suffering and the others are the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. "Suffering" takes oppression as its meaning; it refers to the retribution of the three realms of existence.

"Origin" takes summoning and inducing as its meaning; it refers to the afflictions of views and thought. "Cessation" takes empty exhaustion as its meaning; it refers to the nature of partial truth. "Path" takes proceeding toward as its meaning;
it refers to the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment. As for saying they are "non-existent": if there were suffering and origin, then there would be cessation.

If suffering does not arise, how can the Path and Cessation be established? Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
And the verse from the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā Sūtra* says: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without nature; it is the ultimate emptiness, suchness."

"Knowledge and attainment" refers to the two emptinesses of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). They are subsumed within the two types of selflessness: the contemplation of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the objective realm of the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the objective realm of the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). It is also called "non-existence" (*abhāva*):

not only is the knowing wisdom that realizes emptiness unattainable, but the principle of emptiness that is known is likewise extinguished. As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "The five dharmas and the two types of selflessness."
All are entirely unobtainable. It further states: "To be far removed from what is known by wisdom, and the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), is liberation.

This serves as a concluding statement. It means that within emptiness, each and every mundane and supramundane phenomenon is non-existent, because according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are empty and fundamentally lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that could be apprehended.
Thus, among the twenty kinds of emptiness in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, all phenomena— [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*

Emptiness. The emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). The *Śūraṅgama-śūnyatā*. Within the *ālayavijñāna*, there is nothing that is not "not-so" (non-existent), from the seven elements (*dhātu*), the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), up to the conditions, the truths, the wisdom, the perfections (*pāramitā*), and even the ten titles and four virtues. As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
"The non-arising of all phenomena is the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). One should simply observe the four neighbors within the two cities of the twelve snow mountains.
Discarding frost and ice, existing in the morning and vanishing by evening—when seeking for traces and forms, what could there be? (This is precisely empty space and the unconditioned.
Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, the mind is without hindrance; because there is no hindrance...
There is no fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate nirvana.
Because the Bodhisattva relies on this *prajñāpāramitā*, the Heart of Supreme Emptiness, they give rise to the practice of contemplative observation.
Thus, their mind becomes free from the obstructions and hindrances of karma, like shedding armor in battle; their mind is devoid of the fear of birth and death.
It is like the commutation of a death sentence; the mind is free from delusion, affliction, and inverted perceptions. It is like awakening from a dream.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *mahāparinirvāṇa*, which here is translated as "Great Parinirvāṇa. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*, which transforms birth and death.

"Extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to *vimukti* (liberation), which transforms karmic fetters. "Crossing over" (*pāra*) refers to *prajñā* (wisdom), which transforms delusion. This is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore—

It is quiescent emptiness. Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday" (this refers to the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation).
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
That upon which all Buddhas rely is this one reality alone; the other two are not true.

*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—in the language of Tang, this means "Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Rightly Awakened. "Rightly Awakened" (*saṃbodhi*) refers to the realization of truth through the wisdom of principle (*li-zhì*).

"Perfectly Equal" (*samyak*) refers to the comprehension of conventionality through the wisdom of phenomena (*shi-zhì*). "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) refers to the unobstructed wisdom that directly penetrates the Middle Way.

It is the One Truth. To be in accord with it is called "attainment. Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Even the realization of the Way is without attainment, for the fundamental nature is already perfect.
It further states: "Ordinary beings and all Buddhas are alike like the appearance of flowers in the sky" (this refers to the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation).
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great mantra of spiritual power, a great mantra of illumination, an unsurpassed mantra, and a mantra equal to the unequaled.
It is able to eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
The cause and effect of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are based upon this for cultivation and realization; thus, Prajñā is the secret mantra, and Pāramitā is the esoteric mantra.

This explains the names of the five mantras. They are like military warrants, royal edicts, imperial decrees of favor, and precious seals, each possessing the benefit of liberating one from suffering and attaining happiness.
Their singular transformative power reaches the ultimate peak, and they are called the Great Deity.

This is the *prajñā* of words and letters (*nāma-prajñā*). It transforms the ordinary into the holy, eliminates perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), and removes the suffering of the *kalpa*-turbidity.

It delivers those of the Hīnayāna teachings and is the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). It is the true dharma-joy, universally illuminating and unimpeded; thus it is called the "Great Radiance" (*mahā-vidyā*). This is the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*).

It transforms the small into the great, eliminates perceptions of sensation (*vedanā-saṃjñā*), and removes the suffering of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāluṣya*). It delivers those of the Initial Teachings and is the wondrous observation.

Wisdom (*jñāna*). The joy of the Dharma that is not in vain. Surpassing the heights of the three realms of humans and devas, it is called "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*); this is the *prajñā* of the objective realm.

Through the empowerment of mantras, it perfects the ultimate reality (*niṣpannakrama*), eliminating conceptualization, the turbidity of afflictions, and suffering; it delivers those of the Final Teaching. It is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), the true joy of the Dharma.

Honored equally by the four classes of ordinary beings and sages, it is called "Equal to the Unequaled" (*asamasama*); this is the *prajñā* of the retinue. Through the empowerment of mantras, it is gradual.

It is perfected all at once. Setting aside the notion of practice, sentient beings suffer in solitude; those who are taught by the sudden teaching are delivered. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom does not lack the joy of the Dharma;
it penetrates to the very source of the five dharmas, which is called Prajñāpāramitā—namely, the Prajñā of the True Mark (Lakṣaṇa-prajñā).
The incantation is universally perfected and complete; it eliminates consciousness and perception, the affliction of the impurity of life, and delivers those of the Perfect Teaching.

It is the pure wisdom of the Dharma-realm, the great Dharma-joy of True Suchness that is neither deceptive nor divergent. Just as with the *pulu* (parasitic wasps) and others, how could this be an empty teaching or a mere incantation?
Therefore, the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken.
It is spoken as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. The first four [terms] are the particulars;
this "Prajñā" (Wisdom) is the general [term]. Together they constitute five. Their names and characteristics are found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only).

The non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are comprised of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*). Their essence and function reside in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.

Suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the prose (*gadya*), the verse (*geya*), and all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are suchness. Within this, first there is a brief indication, followed by the formal exposition.

*Gate*: "Go" means to transcend. It refers to personally abandoning attachments and hindrances, transcending into the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*), departing from this shore, and crossing over to the middle stream.
This is the great mantra of the words. Furthermore, the reason it is repeated as *gate* again is: [as follows].
This means causing others to abandon the two attachments and the three obstacles, to cross over the three emptinesses, and to leave the shore of birth and death—the flow of afflictions.
This is the mantra of great illumination and the word "pāra," meaning "to reach the other shore.

That is to say, one personally abandons the two attachments and the three obstacles, crosses over and enters the two emptinesses and the three emptinesses, does not dwell in the middle stream, and ultimately reaches the other shore. This is...
The unsurpassed mantra of the realm. "Saṃgha" means universal, collective, and total.
It signifies universally causing both self and others to exhaust the two attachments and three obstacles, and to cross over into the two emptinesses and three emptinesses.

All sentient beings of the nine realms shall collectively abide nowhere within the four currents, reaching directly to the shore of nirvāṇa. This is the retinue; it is the mantra of the Peerless Equal One. Bodhi.
It is the fruit of perfect enlightenment. It refers to reaching the place of the other shore.

What kind of retribution is obtained such that it causes all those within the *dharmadhātu*, whether enemies or kin, to fully realize the fruit of unsurpassed *bodhi*? This is the *prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-mantra* of the true mark. *Svāhā*.
"Swift and complete accomplishment" means the fulfillment of the three types of awakening and the perfection of the five wisdoms. *Laṅkā...* [text fragment]
Yan said: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart and attain supreme enlightenment;
thus one knows that the merit of the Heart Sūtra and its Heart Mantra is so majestic and sublime that no person can name it."
The eulogy at the conclusion of the brush reads:
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras and the Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra are but mind-only;
The fundamental Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrous nature of True Suchness. With a single glance, one looks away from delusion; The great earth returns to its true state.
